title: Investigation into Iron Age bog body finds death by deliberate decapitation | CNN
text:
Source: CNN

An investigation into a 2,000-year-old bog body discovered in Northern Ireland has revealed that the remains belonged to a young Iron Age woman who likely died by deliberate decapitation in what may have been part of a ritualized killing.

The Ballymacombs More Woman, as she is known, was originally found in a quiet village northwest of Belfast in 2023.

She has been described by experts as an importantexample of a bog body – ancient remains exceptionally preserved due to a mummification-like process that naturally occurred in the cool, acidic conditions of northern Europe’s wetlands.

Belfast’s Ulster Museum shared what scientists know about the woman’s life and death at a public event on Monday modeled on a modern-day coroner’s inquest, which was overseen by one of Northern Ireland’s senior coroners.

A team of archaeologists and specialists in biology, textiles and environmental science assembled at the museum on Monday to participate in the public event and contribute detailed analysis.

Melanie Giles, an archaeologist and professor at the University of Manchester who specializes in the Iron Age and has a wealth of research centered around bog bodies of the period, contributed her expertise during the investigation.

Giles told CNN that formal burials were extremely rare in Iron Age Ireland, and so archaeological finds like the Ballymacombs More Woman are crucial to understanding more about people’s lives at the time.

“We know that women were very important and powerful in Iron Age society, even at her young age,” Giles said. “However, she died a violent death, which leaves us with many questions still to explore.”

“We don’t know if she was being punished or whether she was an innocent captive, a hostage or a scapegoat but the swift manner of her death suggests to me she was a sacrifice or even a sacred emissary to the gods,” Giles added.

While much of the skeleton was remarkably preserved upon excavation, the body was notably without its skull.

Analysis by Eileen Murphy, a professor and archaeologist from Queen’s University Belfast, suggested the woman likely endured sharp-force trauma to the vertebra located in the upper portion of the neck. Murphy’s evidence also indicated that two blows were likely delivered from the right, which may have completely severed the woman’s head.

Murphy said that flexed knees and the apparent position of the woman’s left foot and toes implied that she may have been kneeling in her final moments when dealt the fatal blows.

Murphy concluded that the woman likely collapsed where she was killed, as the torso’s position was consistent with a backwards collapse and rotation of the body after the decapitation.

The investigation heard expert evidence that the woman’s death likely had a ritualistic aspect, with former Keeper of Irish Antiquities Eamonn Kelly noting that a closer examination of early mythological material relating to the period would shed further light on this point.

While human sacrifice and ritualistic killing is often explored through literature associated with the Iron Age, some experts doubt that there is enough reliable evidence to ever name it as a cause of death.

“It is difficult to archaeologically distinguish ‘ritual’ from other types of violence,” Roy van Beek, assistant professor at Wageningen University in the Netherlands – who was not part of the inquest – told CNN in response to the findings.

“I know that some researchers have linked Irish bog bodies with kingship and sovereignty in the past, but personally I have not seen any convincing evidence for this – I find it speculative,” he said, adding that more research is required before a definitive conclusion can be drawn.

Nevertheless, van Beek described Ballymacombs More Womanas “an important find indeed.” He noted that the large majority of known bog bodiesin northern Europe had been discovered in the distant past, thereforehad not been investigated with as rigorous professionality as this one, or had only done so much later when key evidence may have been lost.

“This find provides an important opportunity to use a variety of modern techniques on this recently found body, and also to investigate the findspot itself in detail,” the expert said.

“Specialistic research on the body itself could provide a wealth of new information,” he added.

In his closing remarks, coroner Joe McCrisken emphasized the value of the exercise in developing historical knowledge, but also in sharing the story of a female victim of violence otherwise long forgotten.

“Although separated from us by more than 20 centuries, she was once a living member of her community, and the investigation sought to restore, insofar as possible, an understanding of her life, death and place in history,” the coroner said.
